arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: the side that brought the case's counsel argued that statutory words, purpose, and results all matter when construing the law.
The government's counsel emphasized that the statute defines qualifying offenses by the maximum term prescribed by law.
Justices debated whether the present tense in the statute refers to the time of the prior offense or the current sentencing date.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case asks how courts count prior convictions when state laws change sentencing rules.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on April 25, 2011.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 3, lines 7-17

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the court to count his prior convictions based on the law in effect when he committed them.
The government wants the court to count his prior convictions based on the current maximum sentence.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 20, lines 47-29

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues that the statute requires looking at the law that existed when the prior offense occurred.
The government argues that the statute refers to the maximum term prescribed by law at the time of sentencing.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 20, lines 47-29

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Ginsburg asked if the state prescribes a ten-year maximum for the defendant because the law change was not retroactive.
Justice Sotomayor questioned the logic of punishing someone for activity that was considered less serious at the time of the crime.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case determines how courts calculate criminal history scores for federal sentencing. It affects the length of prison sentences for defendants with prior state convictions. The outcome clarifies the interaction between state sentencing laws and federal sentencing guidelines.
